cards.body:
The Indian River County Sheriffs Office announced the arrest of Matthew Waggle in connection with the fatal shooting of Dawn Kriskewic on First Street in Vero Beach early Sunday morning. Investigators believe Waggle traveled by bus to Orlando and then used an Uber to reach Vero Beach, where he allegedly shot Kriskewic and left the scene just 15 minutes later using the same method of transportation. Sheriff Eric Flowers said Waggle was there for 10 or 15 minutes tops and murdered her in cold blood in the street.

Flowers credited the Flock license plate reader system for helping locate Waggle. Without Flock, the sheriff said, he would not be standing there four days later announcing Waggle was in custody in West Virginia. Flowers said the system helped get a murderer behind bars and off the streets.

Waggle was found at a motel in West Virginia. The gun used in the shooting belonged to Waggles ex-wife, who was at the same hotel. Detectives are questioning whether she knew his plans, but she is not currently facing any charges.
cards.headline: License plate readers helped track Vero Beach murder suspect to West Virginia, sheriff says
cards.teaser: Matthew Waggle was arrested at a West Virginia motel in connection with the fatal shooting of Dawn Kriskewic on First Street in Vero Beach early Sunday morning.

hero.body:
The Indian River County Sheriffs Office released body cam footage showing U.S. Marshals arresting Matthew Waggle at a motel in West Virginia on Wednesday night. Waggle is accused of killing his ex-girlfriend, Dawn Kriskewic, in Vero Beach last Sunday. The video captures officers shouting commands during the arrest.

Kriskewics body was discovered in front of her home on First Street in Vero Beach. She had been shot to death. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said Waggle murdered her in cold blood in the street. Kriskewic had told her co-workers at a hair salon that if Waggle called or showed up, she wanted nothing to do with him and they should tell him she was not there.

Investigators believe Waggle traveled to Vero Beach from Orlando using an Uber, stayed just long enough to kill Kriskewic, and then left town in another Uber. At a news conference Thursday, Flowers explained how the arrest unfolded. The body cam video shows officers placing Waggle in handcuffs at the motel.

Waggle remains in jail in West Virginia as authorities in Florida work on extraditing him back to Indian River County. Marshals arrested him Wednesday night after investigators quickly identified him as a person of interest following the Sunday shooting.

hero.body:
Paige O'Donnell has legally surrendered the 36 Border Collies rescued from her Palm City home, the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast confirmed Friday, clearing the way for the dogs to be adopted or fostered once they are healthy enough. O'Donnell faces 72 charges in what the shelter calls the worst animal hoarding case it has ever seen. The dogs were rescued from her hoarded home in Palm City earlier this month after a WFLX investigation helped renew the sheriff's office probe into the case.

Deputies found the dogs living in deplorable conditions, with fur matted with feces and debris. Court documents show O'Donnell exhibited deceptive behavior during the investigation, blaming strong odors on missed trash collection and old seafood. The rescued Border Collies are now undergoing what shelter staff call medical grooming, a process that involves carefully shaving severely matted fur while checking for injuries and infections underneath. Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, said staff shaved 9 pounds off of one dog filled with feces and urine. Fisher said some dogs arrived with metal and glass fragments trapped in their fur, including lots of pieces of metal, rusted metal, sharp metal, that have been stuck in their fur, along with shards of glass.

Cesar Perea, associate vice president of rescue for American Humane Society, said the emotional and physical recovery process for animals often begins quickly once they are removed from dangerous conditions. As soon as you start providing care, you immediately start to see the animal's personality come out, Perea said. When they were in that situation, they were completely shut down. Perea said trauma in rescued animals can appear as emotional shutdown, inactivity and fear, but he has seen dramatic turnarounds in many hoarding cases across the country. Within two weeks, you wouldn't even recognize that animal, Perea said. They start getting a little more active and joyful. They start behaving like the pets that they're meant to be.

Adoption applications will be available on the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast website and Facebook page beginning Sept. 1. Staff will complete thorough medical testing and evaluations so adopters receive clear information about any long-term needs before placement decisions are made. The dogs also will be prepared for spay and neuter services, microchipping and vaccinations on a phased schedule alongside animals already in the shelter's care. The case has prompted legislative action from State Rep. Meg Weinberger, R-Palm Beach Gardens, who is pushing for a mandatory dog breeder registry in Florida following the Palm City rescue.

During the initial rescue, staff found "lots of pieces of metal — rusted metal, sharp metal — that have been stuck in their fur, along with shards of glass."
